Putting It Together — A Macro Dashboard for Traders

Compare growth, inflation and financial indicators in a documented worksheet, without treating a regime label as a trading instruction.

By Anuga Weerasinghe

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

Source check: 2026-10-18. FRED, BEA GDP and BLS CPI source definitions; no investment-performance validation or professional review.

QUICK ANSWER
Putting It Together — A Macro Dashboard for Traders?

Compare growth, inflation and financial indicators in a documented worksheet, without treating a regime label as a trading instruction. Growth and inflation can form a four-quadrant descriptive worksheet if the measures are defined. Record the source, units and dates of each economic series; check revisions before comparisons.

The four-quadrant regime framework

A four-quadrant worksheet can classify selected observations by whether growth and inflation are rising or falling. Define the measures first: real GDP growth, a survey measure and a monthly release are not interchangeable, and inflation levels differ from changes in the inflation rate. A quadrant is a descriptive simplification, not an asset-allocation rule. Interest rates, starting valuations, supply shocks and expectations can produce different asset returns within the same label.

Building a personal dashboard

FRED provides economic time series and links to their sources and releases. Start a practice dashboard by selecting a few series relevant to a specific question, then record each series' units, frequency, observation date and release date. Check revisions and definitions before comparing values. A dashboard is an aid to study; no measured percentage of useful information or advantage over other traders is established here.

The weekly ritual

For a hypothetical study, choose a review date and record selected yields, exchange rates and price indices. Keep observation dates separate from release dates: GDP is not measured weekly, and later revisions can change the growth story. Record what was actually available at the time. Comparing a later revised series with an earlier trading decision can introduce look-ahead bias.

Don't over-trade macro

A macro label cannot determine an appropriate position size or entry time. Scheduled releases can affect prices quickly even when the underlying economic series changes slowly. Compare alternative explanations and unfavorable cases; a dashboard neither proves causation nor guarantees investment outcomes.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Growth and inflation can form a four-quadrant descriptive worksheet if the measures are defined.
Record the source, units and dates of each economic series; check revisions before comparisons.
A dated log separates observations from releases and later revisions.
A regime label is not a position-sizing, allocation or timing instruction.
Check Your Understanding

Answer all 4 questions to complete this lesson.

1. The descriptive worksheet in this lesson classifies:
Guaranteed returnsSelected growth and inflation directionsCorrect trade sizesFuture prices
2. Which combination best describes stagflation?
Strong growth + high inflationStrong growth + low inflationWeak or stagnant growth + high inflationWeak or stagnant growth + low inflation
3. Why record release dates as well as observation dates?
To guarantee a profitTo know what information was available at the decision timeTo remove market riskTo predict every revision
4. Which resource is the St. Louis Fed’s economic-data database?
BloombergReuters EikonFREDCap IQ
Submit & complete lesson
Answer notes
The descriptive worksheet in this lesson classifies: Options: Guaranteed returns; Selected growth and inflation directions; Correct trade sizes; Future prices. Correct answer: Selected growth and inflation directions. Why: The selected measures define a description, not a forecast.
Which combination best describes stagflation? Options: Strong growth + high inflation; Strong growth + low inflation; Weak or stagnant growth + high inflation; Weak or stagnant growth + low inflation. Correct answer: Weak or stagnant growth + high inflation. Why: Stagflation combines weak or stagnant economic activity with high inflation. Inflation need not accelerate every month; its level differs from a change in the inflation rate.
Why record release dates as well as observation dates? Options: To guarantee a profit; To know what information was available at the decision time; To remove market risk; To predict every revision. Correct answer: To know what information was available at the decision time. Why: Later releases and revisions must not be treated as knowledge available earlier.
Which resource is the St. Louis Fed’s economic-data database? Options: Bloomberg; Reuters Eikon; FRED; Cap IQ. Correct answer: FRED. Why: St Louis Fed's free database.
